draftedLabels: Watercolor and graphite register the changing tones around Cremieu, where the sky’s light appears to spread across the terrain in quick, loose marks.
Shadows move across the landscape as the title directs attention to their passage, making sunlight visible through what it leaves darkened.
The etched pond and rocky banks place still water beneath an open sky, recording weather through the light and shade laid across the ground.
Graphite and watercolor build a small outdoor view in which atmospheric conditions are carried by the wash, from pale air to darker passages.
The distant Sabine Hills are mapped with pen, graphite, and watercolor, while the broad interval between Civitella and Rocca Santo Stefano makes air and visibility part of the scene.
Printed in red, the palo verde trees stand against a spare desert setting where heat, dryness, and hard light are conveyed through the etched line.
rewrittenLabels: The street holds its buildings after the people have left it. In the albumen print, the road itself becomes the record of passage.
A numbered section of canal company ground reads as infrastructure without its workforce. The photograph fixes an industrial site in the interval after activity.
Houses line the canal bank, their façades facing water with no one at the windows or along the edge. Etching reduces the place to a spare arrangement of dwelling, bank, and canal.
The convent is named as an interior place, but its printed architecture carries the scene. Aquatint deepens the sense of rooms and passages left to their surfaces.
A hallway leads toward a bedroom, marking domestic use through doors, walls, and a route through the house. With no occupant visible, the lithograph makes the passage feel recently cleared.
The church doorway stands as a threshold after entry or before return. Its etched lines keep attention on the opening, where absence is most sharply felt.
Railway tracks and their built setting point to movement that has already continued elsewhere. The albumen print leaves the rail line as evidence of departure rather than arrival.
The hotel is identified by place and plate number, an address made impersonal by the photographic record. Its exterior remains while the travelers associated with it are not shown.
The station is built for arrivals and departures, yet the photograph holds on the structure between them. Longueau's rail architecture appears waiting without a visible crowd.
Coal piers and harbor facilities remain after the labor and traffic they require have moved out of view. The photograph treats the waterfront as a set of working traces without workers.
The rail yard is a field of tracks, cars, and industrial distance, organized around transit. Printed years after it was photographed, the image also preserves a moment already gone from the yard.
Church and street meet in a small watercolor view with no figure to occupy the route. The empty street turns the built place into a remainder of communal life.
